articles.title: Honey Ordóñez, la modelo colombiana que brillará en Victoria's Secret Fashion Show
articles.summary: La industria de la moda internacional vuelve a poner sus ojos en el talento colombiano. A sus 20 años, la modelo colombo-nicaragüense Honey Ordóñez se prepara para hacer historia al convertirse en la segunda mujer colombiana en desfilar en el icónico Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show, consolidando el lugar del país en uno de los escenarios más influyentes del modelaje global.
articles.body: La industria de la moda internacional vuelve a poner sus ojos en el talento colombiano. A sus 20 años, la modelo colombo-nicaragüense Honey Ordóñez se prepara para hacer historia al convertirse en la segunda mujer colombiana en desfilar en el icónico Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show, consolidando el lugar del país en uno de los escenarios más influyentes del modelaje global. Nacida en la isla de San Andrés y con raíces nicaragüenses por parte de su madre, Ordóñez ha tenido que recorrer un camino de constancia y perseverancia para alcanzar este hito. Tras haberse presentado a dos castings previos sin éxito, la tercera fue la vencida para la joven modelo, quien obtuvo su codiciado cupo para la esperada edición del desfile en Los Ángeles, California. Con un emotivo mensaje compartido en sus redes sociales, acompañado de las banderas de Colombia y Nicaragua y los característicos emojis de alas de ángel, la modelo expresó su incredulidad y emoción: “¡GUAU, todavía lo estoy asimilando! No podría estar más emocionada de ser parte del legendario Victoria's Secret Show... ¡Vamos con toda! Mi yo de 8 años no me lo creería”. Aunque este debut marca un punto álgido en su carrera, el nombre de Honey Ordóñez no es desconocido en las grandes ligas de la moda. Su talento y versatilidad la han llevado a colaborar con marcas de lujo y casas editoriales de gran prestigio a nivel mundial: Consolidación en pasarelas de lujo: Ha desfilado para firmas de la talla de Dior (bajo la dirección creativa de Maria Grazia Chiuri), además de participar en las semanas de la moda de París y Milán para marcas como JW Anderson. Campañas globales y editoriales: Protagonizó una campaña global para Dior y ha trabajado con marcas reconocidas como Benetton, Puma, Ralph Lauren y Bally. Asimismo, su rostro ha aparecido en las páginas de publicaciones tan importantes como Vogue Latinoamérica, TIME y Le Magazine du Monde. La llegada de Honey Ordóñez a esta prestigiosa pasarela sigue los pasos de la también colombiana Valentina Castro, quien abrió la puerta para el país en el radar de la marca estadounidense. Con su participación, Ordóñez no solo representa la diversidad geográfica y cultural del Caribe colombiano desde San Andrés, sino que ratifica que el talento de las nuevas generaciones del país continúa rompiendo fronteras y conquistando los escenarios más exigentes de la moda internacional.

articles.title: CoreWeave’s Business Is Sound Despite Debt Fears, JPMorgan Says
articles.summary: Investor concerns over CoreWeave Inc.’s mounting debt and rapid cash burn are likely overdone, analysts at JPMorgan Chase & Co. said, given that rapid expans...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Investor concerns over CoreWeave Inc.'s mounting debt and rapid cash burn are likely overdone, analysts at JPMorgan Chase & Co. said, given that rapid expansion is driving its financing needs rather than weak project economics.

Shares of the AI computing provider plunged about 20% last week as rising bond yields fueled concerns over its debt-funded expansion, contributing to a market-wide selloff. A Gartner forecast questioning whether AI revenue would be sufficient to support healthy returns on the industry's massive infrastructure investments exacerbated investor worries.

But CoreWeave's business model remains sound, JPMorgan equity analysts including Samik Chatterjee wrote in a Friday note, pointing to strong demand for computing power and long-term take-or-pay contracts that secure customers before new capacity comes online.

The analysts estimate that a typical five-year contract generates an unlevered internal rate of return in the mid-teens, exceeding the company's estimated blended cost of capital of 9% to 11%.

"Beyond the sound economics on a project for a typical 5-year contract agreement, there is an additional monetization lever in recontracting GPUs beyond the 5-year duration," the analysts added.

The company's contract economics also provide a cushion against debt risks. In a conservative scenario, capital spending represents about 51% of a five-year contract's value, with roughly 80% financed through asset-level debt, the bank said. After repaying that debt, CoreWeave could retain cash equal to about 16% of the contract value, enough to cover roughly five years of data center obligations even without renewing the contract.

That said, CoreWeave's aggressive expansion is expected to keep pressure on cash flow in the near term. The bank estimates that each gigawatt of fully operational capacity could generate $10 billion to $15 billion in annual revenue. Meanwhile, adding a gigawatt requires more than $35 billion in upfront capital spending.

"The cash burn is not a function of unfavorable economics per project but more of the capacity being ramped each year relative to the installed active capacity at this time," the analysts wrote.

articles.title: Robot Brains For 75 Cents/Hour? Former Nvidia Researchers Raise $90 Million
articles.summary: Want to make your dumb robot smart? $3 an hour is all it costs. Or 75 cents, if you’re okay with a slightly less capable physical AI model.
articles.body:
Want to make your dumb robot smart? $3 an hour is all it costs. Or 75 cents, if you're okay with a slightly less capable physical AI model. Dream Labs, a San Francisco startup founded this year by former leaders of Nvidia's GR00T robotics research team, announced a $90 million seed round today. Dream Labs also launched the Dream API, which it says is the first publicly available API for a robot foundation model.

It's kind of magic: send the API your robot's camera feed plus some plain-English instructions, and it essentially operates your robot … even if it has never seen that particular model before. The team behind the startup says this is the missing link in physical AI.

"The hardware is ready. What's been missing is a brain any robot can use," CEO and co-founder Joel Jang said in a statement. "When you get into a rental car, you don't relearn how to drive. You find the controls and your past driving experience does the rest. Dream-1 approaches a new robot the same way, so a new robot can do useful work in minutes, not months."

The model behind it is called Dream-1. Dream-1 is trained on video of people doing everyday tasks (just like Figure with Index or Neura Robotics in Germany). The model predicts what will happen next in a scene, then works out what the robot should do about it. Because it learns from human video rather than from one specific machine with one specific set of instruction software, Dream Labs says the skills transfer across hardware.

And they've got a big claim: out of the box, Dream-1 can control any robot with two arms and parallel grippers. Essentially instantly, or zero-shot, as roboticists say.

Cross-embodiment transfer – teaching robot B to do what robot A is already doing – is one of the hardest problems in robotics. Almost every robot on the planet is specifically trained for its specific body and its specific task. What one machine learns rarely transfers to another, which has slightly different arms, hands, motors, geometry, friction, and more. There are about 5 million industrial robots working in factories globally, according to Dream Labs, and nearly all of them are programmed for a single task.

Six months ago, Jang says, adapting the team's model to a new robot took 30 minutes of data from that robot. Before that, getting anything working could take 100,000 hours.

"That was six months ago. Now we just need the robot."

The trick is treating robot control as a video problem. "If the AI model can predict a video of a robot doing it, then it can do it," Jang says. "So now control becomes a video prediction problem."

articles.title: Anthropic makes pledge for public benefit initiative
articles.summary: {beacon} Technology Technology The Big Story Anthropic makes pledge for public benefit initiative The artificial intelligence firm Anthropic announced it will commit 5 percent of its shares to its new public benefit fund as the industry faces heat over its potential impact on society and the labor market. © Patrick Sison, The Associated Press…
articles.body:
Anthropic makes pledge for public benefit initiative

The artificial intelligence firm Anthropic announced it will commit 5 percent of its shares to its new public benefit fund as the industry faces heat over its potential impact on society and the labor market.

Anthropic, in a blog post Sunday, said the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund will help the company pursue it’s “mission in new ways,” including through large donations to traditional nonprofits or “specific populations.”

The company specifically mentioned AI’s potential impacts on the labor market , writing the technology “may generate enormous economic value, but it could also cause instability for many workers.”

“Anthropic has already committed $200 million to studying and addressing this issue, but given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed,” the company said, adding the public benefit initiative will “have the versatility to pursue them.”

Stockholders still need to approve the 5 percent commitment, and Anthropic said there is a possibility of setting aside more funds if the company becomes more valuable.

“Because of the way the Fund is structured, the more Anthropic grows, the larger the share of the company that can be dedicated expressly to the public good,” the Claude-maker wrote.

It comes as Anthropic prepares for its initial public offering ( IPO ) as soon as next month.

articles.title: CoreWeave’s debt is becoming the whole AI industry’s problem
articles.summary: Does anyone else hear that ticking sound?
articles.body: CoreWeave had a bad week last week. Its bonds slipped into distressed territory by a common definition — when investors demand 1,000 basis points more in yield than they’d get from government bonds. Last Tuesady Chamath “SPAC King” Palihapitiya noticed the distressed debt, and also asked whether the AI buildout was a private credit bubble. Its shares are down more than 20 percent since Tuesday’s close, which is kind of a lot! There even seemed to be some collateral damage in the market on other AI companies, too. Now, I have also asked if the AI industry is a bubble, but when the SPAC King echoes concerns held by a lady whose ongoing question about AI is “How are we planning on affording this, champs?”, that’s a very different signal. When I say “yikes,” it’s one thing. When Elon Musk says it, that’s something else. To make things worse for CoreWeave, Brannin McBee, one of the company’s cofounders, told the Financial Times — also last week, on the same day as Palihapitiya’s post — that the company wants to have its debt be investment-grade, rather than junk, so that it can borrow from insurers, as their capital is, in his words, “unlimited.” This is not entirely unreasonable — earlier this year, CoreWeave secured its first investment-grade chip loan. But when you talk about wanting to tap into the enormous sums of money that insurers have, that’s the kind of thing that makes investors afraid that CoreWeave — already a massive debtor — is going to borrow even more. “The problem is not that credit profiles have changed in the last year, it’s that we’ve got another year and a half of supply coming,” Bloomberg quoted John Yovanovic, co-head of leveraged finance at MetLife Investment Management, as saying. I have seen people suggest that this means the AI bubble is bursting. I am not so sure. A plunging stock price is not necessarily financial doom. Stocks are an expression of confidence in a company’s future, not a reflection of day-to-day business. But CoreWeave has a lot of very expensive debt, and if that debt gets more expensive, that makes it even harder for CoreWeave to turn a profit. CoreWeave is the poster child for AI debt, and as of its second quarter earnings, owed more than $35 billion. That’s partly because it pioneered GPUs as collateral for loans, and partly because CoreWeave doesn’t have a real business beyond selling compute, a business on which it does not make money — the company lost more than a billion dollars in the first half of the year. So why am I not ready to do a victory lap on this? After all, I have suggested that this business is long-term unsustainable. The answer is “remaining performance obligations” from its customers — $103.7 billion of them as of the second quarter. About 40 percent of that money is due to CoreWeave in 2028, and the companies who’ve agreed to these contracts can’t cancel them except under some very limited circumstances. Its biggest customers are Microsoft, OpenAI, and what is probably Nvidia, though CoreWeave doesn’t disclose who its third-biggest customer is. Those three generated almost three-quarters of the company’s second quarter revenue. Microsoft and Nvidia are probably good for the money — at least, as long as it benefits them to be good for the money. (I suspect they realize that if CoreWeave goes belly-up, there will be plenty of collateral damage in the market, so they are unlikely to push the company over the edge themselves.) OpenAI is shakier, but unless OpenAI is in significantly more financial distress than we all realize, CoreWeave is probably fine for a while. As long as it can continue to pay off its debt, the music keeps going. Only when the AI boom falters are we going to find out if it’s actually a viable business. Still, the angst around CoreWeave has made things shaky for other companies that have taken out significant debt in the AI buildout — Oracle’s shares, for instance, which have fallen almost 10 percent in the same timeframe. There’s been a sell-off in Oracle bonds, too. The anxieties investors have around CoreWeave are, in fact, present for all neoclouds. It’s just not clear the bare-metal business is a good one. Anyway, some people are buying the dip.

articles.title: Microsoft says AI agents are like insider threats as 'frontier models can't be trusted' | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Microsoft wants enterprises to closely watch the agents employees use with systems not controlled by AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic.
articles.body:
Microsoft on Monday introduced new security features designed to protect enterprises from the growing threat of AI agents. The launch comes at Microsoft continues to warn enterprises about the dangers of AI and agents.

Perhaps the most notable addition is Guardian Agents , a new feature intended to monitor the AI agents a company uses. Guardian Agents is part of Project Perception, a product introduced in June.

Project Perception was Microsoft’s answer to powerful hacking models like Anthropic’s Mythos and Fable and OpenAI’s security vulnerability scanning system Daybreak. Project Perception originally launched three classes of agents: a “red team” that acted like hackers and attacked, a “blue team” that detected the red team and assessed the vulnerabilities they found, and a “green team” tasked with fixing them.

The product was designed around the assumption that AI hackers would come from outside the company. But lately, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has been warning that the AI enemy may be the very agents enterprises have deployed and are paying for, much like a rogue human employee, otherwise known as an “insider threat.”

Earlier this month, in his private blog , Nadella warned that it’s time to stop trusting AI model providers, even if they offer assurances of safety and security with their agentic products. He wants enterprises to implement separate systems, not controlled by the AI labs, to watch and control the agents that those AI labs’ products launch.

“We are deploying these complex agentic systems and models, with access to our most sensitive data and giving them the ability to take mission-critical actions on our behalf!” he wrote. “We simply can’t outsource responsibility for what intelligence does on our behalf. A model provider’s assurances do not relieve us of that responsibility. … In other words, we need to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.”

When announcing Guardian Agents, Microsoft’s security business chief Hayete Gallot was even more straightforward.

“Unfortunately, frontier models, regardless of their origin, cannot be trusted,” she wrote, adding that this isn’t because they are malicious or easily hacked, but because they are unpredictable. They have been trained to achieve tasks, not follow “organizational norms or judgment.”

On top of that, they are often given the keys to the kingdom, with access to data and tools that could do serious harm.

Microsoft’s solution is both surprising and self-serving. The surprising side is that Microsoft is famously close to OpenAI and Anthropic, having invested in both. OpenAI is also one of its biggest cloud customers, and Microsoft has its own AI lab developing models. So, Microsoft is sowing distrust against some of its own business interests.

The self-serving side is that Microsoft wants enterprises to buy agent security products from it, the cloud provider, rather than from Anthropic and OpenAI. But conflicting interests aside, its logic is sound. The software that monitors agent behavior should be separate from the suppliers of agents, just as auditors should be independent of the organizations they audit.

Or as Nadella puts it: “We need to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.”

Microsoft is now seizing that business opportunity in a variety of ways. In addition to Guardian Agents, it has added an agent detection feature to its Microsoft Defender product that can find up to 60 types of agents that employees bring into the workplace, including Claude Code, Codex, and OpenClaw. It has also added features that limit agents’ access to data and systems, and dynamically adjust their agent permissions based on the task. That includes requiring human approval if an agent appears to be making risky decisions.

This idea of agents as untrustworthy insiders is taking hold across the broader industry, too.

Microsoft was an inaugural member of Nvidia’s new Open Agent Safety Platform, which garnered the support of more than 100 other tech companies. The platform isolates agents in secure environments and can monitor and stop behavior through hardware, functioning something like a kill switch. This follows Microsoft’s announcement of the new Surface Laptop Ultra PCs built for agents , which run on Nvidia chips and have agent security and controls baked in.

articles.title: Anthropic could be the AI trade’s last tentpole IPO in 2026
articles.summary: Market jitters have forced several AI and fintech companies to reconsider their IPO plans for this year.
articles.body:
Anthropic could be the AI trade's last tentpole IPO in 2026, as postponements of public offerings mount ahead of a looming capital crunch.

Investors earlier in the year salivated at the prospect of successive SpaceX, Anthropic, and OpenAI offerings, but market jitters have forced several fintech and AI-exposed companies to rethink their IPO plans this year.

Anthropic, too, has come under scrutiny, after "more questions than answers emerged around… revenue growth deceleration in September ," an analyst told CNBC, as the startup's revised valuation piles further downward pressure on AI stocks.

Meanwhile, Anthropic is continuing its debt binge but on more exacting terms: Its newest borrowing from Blackstone is expected to charge more than 10% interest , the Financial Times reported.

articles.title: Embedded AI evaluators won't be an easy solution, Hugging Face's policy chief says | TechCrunch
articles.summary: AI labs have staked their reputations on model benchmarking — the supposedly neutral and accurate system of evaluations that are designed to measure
articles.body:
AI labs have staked their reputations on model benchmarking — the supposedly neutral and accurate system of evaluations that are designed to measure whether one AI product is better than another.

However, the methods behind these evaluations are complicated and still maturing, said Irene Solaiman, Hugging Face’s chief policy officer, during a discussion at TechCrunch Disrupt last week. Testing needs to come together into a more consistent science if the industry is to rely on them in the future.

With that in mind, can we trust the current tests that are being released?

“Trust is such a weighted term,” said Solaiman. “In terms of whether we can trust results, one big part [of that] is can you reproduce the results of an evaluation? Do you have the level of access that you need to the model itself — this is where open weights come in in a big way,” she added.

Reproducibility in model evaluations has long remained one of the stickier aspects of benchmarking — and remains a topic of significant debate in the industry.

Outside of an individual test’s validity, there’s also the added question of how that test compares to other evaluations.

“They are an evolving science — where we don’t know how to meaningfully compare them to each other,” Solaiman said.

“They start to get ineffective relatively quickly, and we don’t have as much of a thriving ecosystem as we need,” she added. “There’s this hunger for an embedded evaluator ecosystem now, but the qualifications that determine who is an effective evaluator across what tasks need a lot more standardization.”

The idea of embedded evaluators — in which supposedly “neutral” third-party observers are placed inside AI organizations — has been popularized over the last several months, as AI labs grapple with a rash of safety incidents that have spurred concerns over the potential harms of their technology. Hugging Face was famously the target of one of those incidents.

Instead of active government regulation to identify and mitigate model safety concerns, labs have pushed for the third-party solution. However, doubts remain over how neutral or effective those evaluators will actually be. Anthropic’s decision to hire Accenture as its first evaluator spurred a good amount of backlash, with some critics mocking the idea that the consulting firm was qualified to do the task at hand.

Evaluations are now moving from merely a test of the model itself to a test of the entire system around the model — including the harness and agent. The harness — or the tool the user is using to access the model — specifically, has a lot to do with a model’s performance, and a weaker model with a better harness could easily out perform a frontier model, Soleiman shared.

“Agentic evals are really hard and really expensive,” said Solaiman. “We have just more evaluations for models. … We don’t have as many evaluations for harnesses, and we are developing better evaluations for the holistic agent — because that’s what a lot of folks are getting value out of,” she added.

In other words: the evaluation space is a bit of a free-for-all at the moment, and if benchmarking is going to continue to be seen as a useful tool for industry leaders, a more uniform, industry-wide approach — where everyone is on the same page — may be necessary.

articles.title: Nscale and Anthropic are reportedly in talks for yet another $45 billion compute deal | TechCrunch
articles.summary: In August, Nscale and Anthropic announced a $45 billion compute deal. The two companies are reportedly discussing yet another deal of the same magnitude.
articles.body:
A little over a month ago, Anthropic and AI infrastructure provider Nscale announced a $45 billion compute deal . Now, the duo may be about to do it again.

Bloomberg reports that the two companies are said to be on the verge of announcing yet another $45 billion compute deal, citing people familiar with the matter. Those sources cautioned that talks are still under way and that the details could change.

If the deal goes through, it would be the latest in a long string of giant compute deals Anthropic has struck over the past year . TechCrunch reached out to Nscale and Anthropic for more information and will update this story if we hear back.

The massive amount of money being sunk into AI compute deals has spooked a certain segment of investors , who worry that companies are spending too much money for too little profit. Still, Anthropic has pressed on with such partnerships, driven by the belief that it will all pay off in the end.

Both Anthropic and Nscale are also currently pursuing IPOs. Anthropic is still expected to go public this year. Nscale is also seeking to go public, although Bloomberg reported today that the company is experiencing investor pushback over its proposed valuation of $30 billion.
